name: Kira Varga

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start: tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm doing a biology degree with a focus on ecology, and so far the week is lectures Monday to Wednesday and lab on Thursday, which I love. I'm in a flat with two girls from my halls, and we cook together on Sundays. I walk to the botanical garden on campus between classes just to breathe. My parents send my rent and food money, so I've only worked a few shifts at the campus cafe for fun.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "AI Plateau". Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at uni, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, fine, then we can stop panicking and spend the attention on climate and nature instead. I'd probably post that on my course group, and half of them would roll their eyes. I like having some tools that help with boring jobs, so I'd say use them where they work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be a bit relieved, but I'd also know the real problems stay the same. Nobody is fixing biodiversity because of AI. My lab demonstrator uses a tool to sort the species photos, and it saves her hours, so that's the kind of small help I imagine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going. I'd use the AI tool for summaries now and then, like I do, and I'd apply for the conservation society's field trip in spring. I'd also try for a summer volunteer place at the wetland reserve outside town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. The degree is going well, and my parents cover everything. If I'm worried about anything, it's the planet, not my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you use an AI tool now and then. What for, exactly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly to turn a long paper into a summary before I read the real thing, and to check my grammar. I never copy what it gives me, because my professor told us it invents citations. I'd say I use it about once a week, like a calculator, not a friend.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the job you picture at the end of the degree?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I want to work in conservation, maybe surveying habitats or doing policy for a wildlife trust. My aunt Marta works for a river trust and she says the pay is low but the work is real. I'm lucky I can afford to go for that kind of job, because my parents would help if I started low.

say: I'd say we can **stop panicking** and spend the attention on climate and nature.
I'd tell my course group to use AI **where it works**, and no further.
think: Privately I'm **relieved**, but the real problems like biodiversity stay the same.
I think small tools that **sort photos** and save hours are the realistic future.
do: Keep using an AI tool **once a week** for summaries, never for copying.
Apply for the conservation society's **spring field trip** and a summer reserve place.
feel: I feel **calm**, because the degree is going well and my parents cover costs.
S0.quote: I use it about once a week, like a calculator, not a friend
fieldNote: Moderate AI use, sensible about its limits; her worry is **ecological** rather than personal.
Her aunt Marta at a river trust shows a realistic view of low-paid **conservation** work.
Parental backing means career choice is free of money pressure, which keeps her **calm**.

steps.text: Keep using an AI summary tool about once a week
Apply for the spring conservation society field trip

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "Steady Disruption". Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at uni, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people should get ready now, since the thinking tasks go first and that's most office jobs. I'd say science will use it too, so we should learn to check it, not worship it. I'd say that in seminars and probably get a debate going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think my area is half exposed: the data analysis and report writing will go to software, but fieldwork and lab work stay human for a while. So the jobs left might be fewer and more field-based. A lot of graduate jobs in ecology are mainly data crunching, and those could shrink.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start learning R and some data skills properly, so I'm the one who checks what the machine produces. I'd take the conservation placement for outdoor skills, and I'd read up on how wildlife trusts use AI. I'd also speak to my aunt Marta about which skills her trust pays for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a bit curious. It's a lot of change, and I want to be on the side of whoever uses it well, not the person who gets replaced.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said fewer graduate jobs might shrink. Who do you think decides that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The funders and the managers do. If a wildlife trust can get its survey data analysed by software, a board will cut the analyst post and say it saved money. I'd want a union or a professional body to argue that the savings go to field staff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any part of you that sees this as good news?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. If the software handles the boring spreadsheet part, I get more time outside, which is why I picked ecology. I just don't trust the bosses to let that happen without being pushed, so I'd want rules about it.

say: I'd tell seminar groups we should **learn to check** AI, not worship it.
I'd say the **thinking tasks** go first, which means most office jobs.
think: I think **data analysis** jobs in ecology could shrink while fieldwork stays human.
I see good news too: software could free **more time** outdoors.
do: Learn **R and data skills** so I'm the person who checks the machine.
Ask my aunt Marta which **skills** her river trust pays for.
feel: I feel **uneasy** but curious, wanting to be on the side that uses it well.
S1.quote: If a wildlife trust can get its survey data analysed by software, a board will cut the analyst post and say it saved money
fieldNote: Her thinking splits her field into **desk analysis** at risk and fieldwork that lasts.
Progressive reflex: wants **rules and unions** so savings reach field staff.
Sees real upside, so the mood is mild: her own plans look **safe enough** if she adds data skills.

steps.text: Learn R and basic data analysis through a society course
Read how wildlife trusts use AI tools in surveys
Ask my aunt Marta which skills her trust pays for

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "AGI by 2028". Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at uni, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, please, nobody is ready, and governments need to act this year. I'd say it online and sign every petition about regulation. Two years is really not enough for anyone to retrain, so we need rules and support for people fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be frightened. My degree finishes in 2029, after AGI is here, and graduate jobs in data and analysis could be gone before I can apply. The fieldwork would stay until 2031, but even that is a few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay on the degree but push towards the hands-on side: field ecology, lab techniques, anything with mud and boots. I'd join the students' climate group, which is already talking about regulation, and write to my local representative. And I'd talk with my parents about what they'd do if their jobs go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'm lucky with money, which matters a lot, but I can't tell what my degree is worth.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What are your parents' jobs, and how exposed are they?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad is a secondary-school teacher in Szeged and my mum is a civil engineer who reviews drawings. Mum's job is much more at risk, because checking drawings is something AI is good at. If my mum's firm cuts her job, that changes what my family can pay for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only two years, would you change anything about your degree?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep it, because ecology needs people in the field. But I'd drop the idea of a long research master's and aim for a practical job early, like a ranger or survey technician. If things are changing that fast, I'd want paid experience over another certificate.

say: I'd say **nobody is ready** and governments must act this year, online and in petitions.
I'd argue we need **rules and support** because two years is too short to retrain.
think: I'm frightened that graduate **data jobs** may be gone before I can apply.
My **mum's** drawing-review job is much more at risk than my own field.
do: Push my degree toward **fieldwork**: field ecology, lab techniques, anything outdoors.
Write to my local representative and join the **climate group**'s regulation campaign.
feel: I feel **anxious**, because I can't tell what my degree will be worth.
S2.quote: If my mum's firm cuts her job, that changes what my family can pay for
fieldNote: Her anxiety centres on **degree value** and her mother's engineering job, not on money today.
She shifts toward **hands-on** ecology, reading exposure correctly from her course.
Political action is her default way to cope when the timeline is **too short**.

steps.text: Write to my local representative about AI regulation
Choose field ecology modules over data-heavy ones
Talk with my parents about what they'd do if Mum's job goes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "AGI by 2031". Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at uni, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a window and we should use it. I'd say people at university should be demanding retraining funds and a say in how it's done. I'd probably help organise something at the students' union.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm still worried but not frozen. Five years means I'd graduate in 2029 and have maybe two years of working before AGI is complete. The hands-on part comes in 2034, so a field job should last a bit longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, build practical skills and try for a ranger or survey technician job right after. I'd save more of what I earn, since my parents won't pay forever. And I'd stay involved in the climate and regulation groups so I'm connected to people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mixed. I'm uneasy about what comes after, but there's time to act, and that makes it a lot easier to carry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your parents won't pay forever. What changes when you're earning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right now I don't think about money. Once I graduate I'd pay my own rent in a shared flat, and I want to put away something every month so I have a cushion when jobs get strange. Even a hundred a month would be a start, as I've never saved before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the students' union actually do about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They could run a retraining fair and push the university to teach people how to work with these systems. They could also lobby the government for a basic income pilot, which my politics tutor says is possible. It's not much, but it makes us feel less alone.

say: I'd say five years is a **window**, and students should demand retraining funds.
I'd help organise something at the **students' union**.
think: I'm worried but **not frozen**, since a field job should last a bit longer.
I'd get about **two years** of working before full AGI is complete.
do: Finish the degree and aim for a **ranger or survey technician** job.
Save **a hundred a month** once I'm earning, since my parents won't pay forever.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about what comes after, but time makes it lighter.
S3.quote: Even a hundred a month would be a start, as I've never saved before
fieldNote: Time shifts her from alarm to **planning**: practical skills, first job, a savings habit.
She admits she has never thought about **money** because her parents have always paid.
Collective action is how she copes: **students' union** and retraining fairs.

steps.text: Save a hundred a month after the first job starts
Take a ranger or survey technician post after graduating
Help the students' union run a retraining fair

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "AGI by 2036". Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at uni, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a good thing, because it gives us time to shape the rules properly. I'd tell friends to keep studying what they love and push for good laws at the same time. I'd want it to be a public conversation, not left to tech companies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel pretty optimistic. A decade is a full career start. I could do the degree, a master's, and a few years in the field before robots reach hands-on work around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the master's I really want, maybe in conservation policy, since that's where people will be needed to decide how to use all this. I'd learn to use AI tools more seriously for research. And I'd get involved in an environmental group that works with policymakers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm. It's the same end point, but with ten years I feel I can steer myself, not just get hit by it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why conservation policy, rather than the lab or field?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because if AI does the analysis, the hard part becomes deciding what to protect and who pays. That's a human argument, and I'd rather be in the room for it. My aunt Marta says policy people at her trust are the ones who get listened to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the difference for you between ten years and five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With five years I'm reacting, and with ten I get to plan. I could finish a master's, work for a few years and still have time to move if things shift. I'd be twenty-nine in 2036, which feels young enough to start over if I have to.

say: I'd say ten years is a **gift**, because we can shape the rules properly.
I'd tell friends to study what they love and push for **good laws**.
think: I feel **optimistic**, since a decade covers a degree, a master's and field years.
I'd rather be **in the room** deciding what to protect.
do: Do a **master's** in conservation policy, where human decisions still matter.
Join an environmental group that works with **policymakers**.
feel: I feel **calm**, as with ten years I can steer.
S4.quote: With five years I'm reacting, and with ten I get to plan
fieldNote: Ten years turns the threat into a **career design** problem; she picks policy where human judgment remains.
Her optimism rests on **money** safety, since her parents can cover a master's.
She uses her aunt as a **real example** of who gets listened to.

steps.text: Apply for a conservation policy master's after the degree
Use AI tools for research notes in the third year
Join an environmental group that talks to policymakers

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one worries me most, because it leaves no time to plan, and my mum's engineering job could go first. What would help is rules before it happens, public money for retraining and a promise that the gains are shared, not kept by a few companies.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I don't want people to think progressive means anti-technology. I want these tools to help us protect nature and cut boring work. I just want ordinary people to have a say, because the decisions are being made in rooms I'm not in.

headlineQuote: I don't want people to think progressive means anti-technology. I want these tools to help us protect nature and cut boring work
portrait: Kira is a 19-year-old **ecology** student whose parents pay for everything, so she studies without money stress.
She uses **AI tools** once a week, like a calculator, and wants to learn to check them.
Progressive and steady, she answers with **rules, unions and petitions** and wants gains shared.
Her mood runs from calm to anxious, peaking in 2028 because her **mother's** job is exposed.
With time she plans a conservation policy master's, aiming to be where human decisions are made.
biggestWorry: She fears **AGI by 2028** most, because there is no time to plan and her mum's job is exposed.
whatWouldHelp: She wants **rules before it arrives**, public retraining money and gains shared with ordinary people.
